alignment.note: Greek uses the substantival articular participle ὁ πιστεύσας ('the one who believed'); Latin and Syriac both recast this as a relative clause (Qui... / ܐܝܢܐ ܕ...), a routine syntactic accommodation since neither language has an exact equivalent of the Greek articular participle.

Greek aorist participle πιστεύσας and Latin future-perfect crediderit both mark anteriority ('having believed' / 'will have believed'), whereas the Syriac ܕܡܗܝܡܢ stands in a participial/present form, expressing the act more aspectually than temporally.

The single Greek passive participle βαπτισθείς is rendered in Latin by a periphrastic future-perfect passive baptizatus fuerit, while in Syriac the verb ܘܥܡܕ is fused with the conjunction (ܘ-) into one token; the alignment reflects this morphological packaging difference.

Greek σωθήσεται and Latin salvus erit both denote 'will be saved' in a soteriological sense, but the Syriac ܚܝܐ (root kh-y-a, 'will live / be made alive') frames salvation as 'life,' a characteristic Syriac idiom that interprets σῴζω through the lexicon of living rather than rescue.

The second substantival articular participle ὁ (...ἀπιστήσας) is again rendered by relative clauses in Latin (qui) and Syriac (ܐܝܢܐ ܕ-, here fused with the conjunction ܘ-), continuing the same construction-level adaptation seen in the protasis.

Greek δέ is a lightly adversative connective rendered by Latin vero ('but, indeed'); the Syriac integrates the adversative force into the conjunctive prefix ܘ- on ܘܐܝܢܐ rather than supplying a discrete particle.

Greek expresses unbelief with a single negative verb ἀπιστήσας; both Latin (non crediderit) and Syriac (ܕܠܐ ܡܗܝܡܢ) analyse this into a negator plus the verb 'believe,' lacking a derived privative verb of disbelief.

The Clementine Vulgate inserts a colon between the two clauses, formalising the antithetical parallelism that the Greek marks only with the raised point and δέ; this is editorial punctuation without textual weight.
